profile.summary: ModernGENA is a DNA language model that adapts the ModernBERT encoder to genomic sequences. It reads DNA split into byte-pair-encoding (BPE) tokens and was pretrained by masked language modelling on 443 vertebrate genome assemblies. It outputs token embeddings that are fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as sequence classification or per-token regression; the authors present it as an efficient baseline for future DNA model work.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; model card: Tokenization, Pretraining corpus; GENA_LM examples README

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ModernGENA is a BERT-style encoder built on ModernBERT. The model card lists RoPE positional embeddings, hybrid local and global attention, pre-norm transformer blocks, GeGLU feed-forward layers and end-to-end unpadding, with FlashAttention for faster inference on compatible hardware. In the published configurations, local attention covers 128 tokens and every third layer uses global attention. Input DNA is tokenised with the 32k BPE vocabulary from GENA-LM over the symbols A, T, G, C and N. Pretraining used masked language modelling on intervals sampled from -16 kbp to +8 kbp around each transcription start site, on both strands, to reduce the weight of simple repeats.

profile.summary: GPN (Genomic Pretrained Network, also called GPN-SS) is a DNA language model that learns from unaligned genome sequences alone. Given a 512-bp DNA window with some positions masked, it predicts the nucleotide at each masked position. Its main use is to score genetic variants without labels: the score is the log-likelihood ratio of the alternate against the reference allele. The published model was trained on Arabidopsis thaliana and seven other Brassicales genomes.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/models/gpn.md introduction; paper Fig. 1 caption; model card title

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GPN is a convolutional neural network, not a transformer. The masked DNA sequence is one-hot encoded with single nucleotides as tokens, then passed through 25 convolutional blocks. Each block has a dilated convolution and a feed-forward layer, with residual connections and layer normalisation; the embedding dimension stays at 512. Training is masked language modelling: 15% of positions are masked and predicted with a cross-entropy loss. To score a variant, only the variant position is masked, and the score is the log-likelihood ratio of the alternate against the reference allele. The authors down-weighted repetitive elements in the loss; the card records a repeat weight of 0.1.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Fig. 1 caption; model card: Some hparams

sections.body: The songlab-cal/gpn repository now covers four model families: GPN, GPN-MSA, PhyloGPN and GPN-Star. This page is about single-sequence GPN. Its published checkpoint is songlab/gpn-brassicales, which uses a seven-token DNA tokenizer. The same family also has an animal promoter model (songlab/gpn-animal-promoter) and a sorghum gene-expression model fine-tuned from gpn-brassicales. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read gpn-brassicales at revision eb9c35d0. The paper analyses are kept in an archive branch, and the maintained training recipe is in recipes/gpn_training. Note that the existing benchmark source (Tang et al. 2025) did not use gpn-brassicales: it evaluated a custom GPN pre-trained on the human reference genome.

profile.summary: ViroHyena is a small family of nucleotide language models built on the Hyena architecture by the authors of the ViroBench viral genomics benchmark. They were pretrained on ViroBlend, a 216 Mbp corpus that mixes human reference, multi-species and viral sequences. The models take nucleotide sequences and serve as baselines in ViroBench for viral taxonomy and host classification from embeddings and for likelihood-based genome modelling.

sections.body: ViroHyena uses the HyenaDNA model type: stacked Hyena layers over a nucleotide vocabulary of 12 tokens and a maximum of 8192 positions. The four checkpoints differ in width and depth, from d_model 128 with 2 layers to d_model 1024 with 20 layers. The cards tag the models for text generation. In ViroBench, classification is done with the backbone frozen: a sequence embedding is extracted and a small MLP head is trained on it. profile.summary: BioFM is a genomic foundation model from M42 Health that reads DNA together with biological context. Its BioToken tokeniser encodes genetic variants and annotated regions (such as genes and regulatory elements) directly in the input, instead of treating DNA as bases only. The model produces embeddings for variants or sequences, which are used with simple classifiers to predict effects on expression, splicing and pathogenicity; it can also generate DNA sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; model card: Model Details; README: Quick Start

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BioFM is a decoder-only (causal) transformer on the Mistral architecture, with 23 layers and hidden size 640. Its input is DNA annotated with BioTokens: tokens that carry variant information and genomic annotations alongside the bases. For a variant, the package builds an upstream and a downstream sequence, each ending at the variant and half the evaluation context long; the downstream one is reverse complemented. Reference and mutated embeddings are each averaged over the two directions and then concatenated, giving a vector twice the embedding size. For plain sequences the embedding is taken from the last token. Downstream predictions use linear probing on these embeddings.

profile.summary: DeepGene is a DNA foundation model that learns from a pan-genome graph rather than a single reference sequence, so that genetic variation across individuals is part of what it sees in pretraining. It is a transformer encoder with rotary position embeddings, built to handle sequences of different lengths. The pretrained model is fine-tuned for sequence classification tasks such as promoter prediction and the Genome Understanding Evaluation (GUE) tasks.

profile.summary: eccDNAMamba is a pretrained model for extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA), circular DNA molecules that carry amplified oncogenes in cancer. It reads full-length eccDNA sequences of 10 to 200 kbp, and copies the start of each sequence onto its end so the model sees across the point where the circle was opened. Fine-tuned versions are used for cancer-associated eccDNA prediction, copy-number level estimation, and telling real from pseudo-eccDNA.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: eccDNAMamba is a bidirectional state-space model: forward and reverse Mamba-2 encoders read the sequence in both directions, with cost linear in sequence length. DNA is tokenised by motif-level byte pair encoding (BPE) with a vocabulary of 4096. To respect the circular shape, a head-tail augmentation appends the first 64 tokens after the end of the sequence. The pretrained backbone is a masked language model (BiMambaForMaskedLM) with 24 layers and d_model 768. For classification, the published fine-tuning code mean-pools the hidden states and adds a two-layer classifier head.

profile.summary: Genomics-FM is a DNA foundation model meant to cut the amount of labelled data that genomic prediction tasks need. It is a BERT-style encoder pretrained on large amounts of unlabelled DNA with an ensemble of tokenisation vocabularies (BPE and 6-mer), then fine-tuned with one task-specific vocabulary on a small labelled set. sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is a BERT masked language model built on the MosaicML BERT code, which uses ALiBi position biases and FlashAttention. During pretraining each sequence is tokenised either with a BPE vocabulary or as 6-mers, and a prompt token marking the vocabulary ([BPE] or [KMER]) and the position scheme ([ALIBI] or [APE]) is put in front of it. Sequences are randomly replaced by their reverse complement half the time. Training masks tokens with a probability of 0.15 for BPE input and 0.15 divided by 6 for 6-mer input, over blocks of 512 tokens, for up to 1,000,000 steps in fp16. For a downstream task the model is fine-tuned with one chosen vocabulary.

profile.summary: MutBERT is a DNA language model for the human genome that is built to learn from genetic variation such as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Instead of training on one reference sequence, it encodes each genome position as a probability over the four bases, taken from allele frequencies in the 1000 Genomes Project. Given a DNA sequence, it outputs per-nucleotide embeddings that can be pooled into a sequence embedding or fine-tuned for classification.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; 2.2 Probabilistic genome representation; README: 4.2 Get the embeddings

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MutBERT is a transformer encoder trained with masked language modelling. It has 12 encoder layers and uses rotary position embeddings (RoPE) and flash attention. Each position in the input is a distribution over the bases: positions without observed variants give the reference base a probability of 1, and variable positions carry the observed allele frequencies. Because the input is a probability matrix and not a token sequence, the usual embedding look-up is replaced by a linear layer, so each position's embedding is a weighted sum of the base embeddings. During pretraining the authors apply temperature scaling to the skewed allele probabilities. The model works at single-nucleotide level with a vocabulary of A, T, C, G and five special tokens. In the README usage example, plain sequences are passed as a one-hot matrix.
sections.source_locator: Paper: 2.1 Model architecture, 2.2 Probabilistic genome representation, 2.3 Tokenization and vocabulary, 2.4; README: 4.2 Get the embeddings

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three pretrained checkpoints share one architecture and differ only in the training data. MutBERT uses probabilistic genomes from the 1000 Genomes Project. MutBERT-Multi uses probabilistic genomes from a 100-species whole-genome alignment. MutBERT-Ref (on Hugging Face, CompBioDSA/MutBERT-Human-Ref) takes one-hot encodings of the hg38 reference and serves as the deterministic baseline. All were trained for 120 000 steps with batch size 2048 and maximum sequence length 512. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read MutBERT at a6cdc94d, MutBERT-Human-Ref at 766be54e and MutBERT-Multi at cbdab668.
sections.source_locator: Paper: 2.1 Model architecture, 2.4 to 2.5; README: 2. Model and Results; model cards: title lines

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors compared MutBERT with DNABERT-2, several Nucleotide Transformer versions and modified MutBERT variants on transcription factor binding sites (from the GUE benchmark), the Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks and eQTL variant effect prediction. For the eQTL task they extended MutBERT's input from 512 to 2048 base pairs and trained an SVM on the embeddings. The authors report that MutBERT ranked among the top models, and that it beat the alternatives in most of the three eQTL distance categories. They note it was pretrained on 4 L20 GPUs for 6 days.

run_guide.summary: Set up the repository environment at a pinned commit, download MutBERT from Hugging Face and compute a mean-pooled and a max-pooled embedding for a short DNA sequence.
prerequisites: conda, to create a Python 3.12 environment.
The requirements file pins torch==2.5.1 and transformers==4.45.2. The README example runs on CPU; GPU type and memory for inference are not stated.
Weights are MIT licensed and not gated. The code repository states no licence.

steps.title: Compute an embedding
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

model_name = "CompBioDSA/MutBERT"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True)

dna = "ATCGGGGCCCATTA"
inputs = tokenizer(dna, return_tensors='pt')["input_ids"]

mut_inputs = F.one_hot(inputs, num_classes=len(tokenizer)).float().to("cpu")  # len(tokenizer) is vocab size
last_hidden_state = model(mut_inputs).last_hidden_state   # [1, sequence_length, 768]

# embedding with mean pooling
embedding_mean = torch.mean(last_hidden_state[0], dim=0)
print(embedding_mean.shape) # expect to be 768

# embedding with max pooling
embedding_max = torch.max(last_hidden_state[0], dim=0)[0]
print(embedding_max.shape) # expect to be 768
PY
steps.explanation: The README 'Get the embeddings' example wrapped in a shell heredoc, with its two comment-only alternative lines left out. It downloads the tokenizer and weights, one-hot encodes the tokens and runs the encoder. For the other checkpoints, change model_name to CompBioDSA/MutBERT-Human-Ref or CompBioDSA/MutBERT-Multi as the README lists them.

profile.summary: OmniNA is a generative foundation model for nucleotide sequences from many species. It was pretrained on 91.7 million DNA and RNA sequences from the NCBI nucleotide database, each paired with its text annotation, so that it learns to write an annotation for a sequence. After fine-tuning, it answers questions about an input sequence in natural language, for example whether it is a promoter, or which species it comes from.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OmniNA uses the LLaMA architecture, an auto-regressive decoder-only transformer. Sequences and annotations share one byte pair encoding tokenizer, built with SentencePiece and trained on nucleotide sequences and wiki-103 text, with 32,001 tokens. Each pretraining example is a prompt with three parts: an instruction, a nucleotide sequence and its annotation, and the model is trained to generate the text. Inputs are capped at 601 tokens. Fine-tuning casts each downstream task as a question and answer: the training file adds a question column, and the model learns to generate the answer.

sections.body: The paper and README describe three sizes. The README table gives OmniNA-66M (8 layers, 8 heads, 66 million parameters), OmniNA-330M (16 layers, 16 heads, 330 million) and OmniNA-1.7B (24 layers, 32 heads, 1.7 billion). Hugging Face holds XLS/OmniNA-66m, XLS/OmniNA-220m and XLS/OmniNA-1.7B. The XLS/OmniNA-220m configuration has 16 layers and 16 heads, the shape the README gives for OmniNA-330M, so the middle checkpoint appears to be the same model under two different size names. The model card read (1.7B) holds only a licence tag. A result should name the Hugging Face checkpoint and revision; this page read 66m at 2c5e876a, 220m at 64ea6ce7 and 1.7B at 73d208a3.

profile.summary: PlantCaduceus (short name PlantCAD) is a DNA language model for flowering plants, pretrained on the genomes of 16 angiosperm species. It reads 512-bp DNA windows one nucleotide at a time, looking at both strands. Its embeddings feed small classifiers that predict translation start and stop sites and splice sites in species it was not trained on, and its masked-base likelihoods give a zero-shot score for how deleterious a single-nucleotide variant is.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: PlantCAD overview; Paper: Abstract, Introduction, Fig. 1 caption

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PlantCaduceus uses the Caduceus architecture, which builds on the Mamba state-space sequence model and adds bi-directionality and reverse complement (RC) equivariance, so both DNA strands are modelled together. It uses single-nucleotide tokens. Pretraining is masked language modelling: 15% of positions in each 512-bp window are masked and the model is trained with cross-entropy loss on them. Following GPN, the pretraining set down-samples noncoding regions and down-weights repeats. Downstream, frozen embeddings train XGBoost or linear classifiers, and the zero-shot score is the log-likelihood difference between the reference and alternate allele at a masked position.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: PlantCAD comes in four sizes, named by their number of Caduceus blocks: PlantCaduceus_l20, l24, l28 and l32, all with a 512-bp input. The model card recommends the largest, l32, for zero-shot scoring. The same repository now also hosts PlantCAD2, a later generation with an 8192-bp input and separate checkpoints (Small, Medium, Large); it is a different model and is not covered here. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; the listing read on 2026-11-26 gives l32 at e624c13c, l28 at 5ac1d5e7, l24 at 8c41e4d5 and l20 at d1b3c7d4.

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForMaskedLM

device = 'cuda:0'
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('kuleshov-group/PlantCaduceus_l32')
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    'kuleshov-group/PlantCaduceus_l32', trust_remote_code=True
).to(device)

sequence = ""

input_ids = tokenizer.encode_plus(
    sequence, return_tensors="pt", return_attention_mask=False,
    return_token_type_ids=False
)["input_ids"].to(device)

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model(input_ids=input_ids, output_hidden_states=True)

embeddings = outputs.hidden_states[-1].to(torch.float32).cpu().numpy()

# Average forward and reverse complement embeddings
hidden_size = embeddings.shape[-1] // 2
forward = embeddings[..., 0:hidden_size]
reverse = embeddings[..., hidden_size:][:, ::-1, :]
averaged_embeddings = (forward + reverse) / 2
print(averaged_embeddings.shape)
PY

profile.summary: SPACE is a DNA model that learns sequence representations by supervised training rather than by masked or next-token prediction. It is trained to predict thousands of genomic profiles, such as chromatin accessibility, transcription factor binding, histone marks and CAGE, from long human and mouse DNA sequences. Its encoder can then be fine-tuned or used as a feature extractor for other DNA tasks, and the full model predicts the profiles themselves.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SPACE (Species-Profile Adaptive Collaborative Experts) keeps the Enformer setup of predicting genomic profiles from DNA, and adds two Mixture of Experts (MoE) parts. A species-aware encoder adds a trainable species embedding and routes each input sparsely across experts, so it can learn both species-specific and shared features. A profile-grouped enhancement decoder uses gated experts to model dependencies between profile types before the human and mouse output heads. The implementation is based on Enformer-Pytorch and Mod-Squad. In the released configuration the input is 131,072 bp, the model width is 1536 with 11 layers and 8 attention heads, the species MoE has 4 experts and the profile MoE has 8, and topk is set to 3.

The training data are the Enformer human and mouse sets, which the authors converted from the Basenji TensorFlow files to H5 and published as the Hugging Face dataset yangyz1230/space. With frozen embeddings on the BEND benchmark they report strong results on chromatin accessibility, histone modification and CpG methylation, but limited effectiveness on the two variant effect tasks. profile.summary: AIDO.DNA, now renamed GB.DNA by its developer GenBio AI, is a large DNA language model meant as a general-purpose encoder of DNA sequence. It reads up to 4,000 nucleotides one base at a time and was pretrained on 10.6 billion nucleotides from 796 species. Its embeddings are fine-tuned or probed for tasks such as gene expression prediction, genome mining, in silico mutagenesis and sequence generation.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; model card: introduction, Tokenization; ModelGenerator backbones: deprecated aliases

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: AIDO.DNA is a BERT-style, encoder-only dense transformer trained with masked language modelling. It uses single-nucleotide tokens from a 5-letter vocabulary (A, T, C, G, N), with a [CLS] token at the start and an [EOS] token at the end of each sequence. The authors updated the BERT design with SwiGLU, LayerNorms and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE). The 7B model has 32 layers, 32 attention heads and hidden size 4352. Its design bet, in the authors' words, is to scale model size while keeping a short 4k context. It was trained for 100000 iterations at global batch size 1024 on 256 H100 GPUs with Megatron-LM, which took 8 days.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Architectural Details, Tokenization, Training Details; bioRxiv abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two pretrained checkpoints are released: a 7B model and a 300M model. Both were first published as AIDO.DNA-7B and AIDO.DNA-300M and are now named GB.DNA-7B and GB.DNA-300M on Hugging Face; the old names still resolve to the new repositories. In ModelGenerator the backbones are gb_dna_7b and gb_dna_300m, and the old names aido_dna_7b and aido_dna_300m remain as deprecated aliases. The 300M card gives no training details of its own and refers to the 7B card. A result should name the checkpoint and its revision; this page read GB.DNA-7B at 5dd948f7 and GB.DNA-300M at a833c560.

profile.summary: Ladon is a foundation model for bulk RNA sequencing of tumours, built by the company Blank Bio. It learns from millions of RNA-seq profiles by reconstructing masked parts of isoform-level expression, and its embeddings are then used to predict patient survival, recurrence and response to treatment. The developers present it as a way to make RNA-based predictions that still hold in clinical trials and cohorts the model was not fitted on.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Ladon is a transformer encoder-decoder of 3 billion parameters. It is pretrained self-supervised, by masked token reconstruction on isoform-level expression profiles, so it can learn from samples without outcome labels. For clinical use the developers then mid-train it with supervision to predict patient and tumour characteristics such as disease stage, age, tumour grade and genomic alterations, together with clinical outcomes. They then discard the prediction heads, freeze the encoder and fit simple outcome models, such as linear Cox survival models, on its embeddings. The report does not describe the layers, tokenisation or training corpus in more detail.

profile.summary: PlantRNA-FM is an RNA language model for plants. It was pretrained on transcript sequences from 1,124 plant species, together with predicted secondary structure and labels for the 5' UTR, coding sequence and 3' UTR. It reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and outputs per-nucleotide embeddings, which the authors fine-tune for tasks such as genic region annotation and translation efficiency, and use to find RNA sequence and structure motifs linked to translation.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PlantRNA-FM is an encoder-only transformer with 12 layers and an embedding dimension of 480. Each nucleotide is one token, and positions are encoded with rotary position embedding. Pretraining used three objectives together: masked nucleotide modelling, in which 20% of nucleotides in each sequence are selected for masking and reconstructed; prediction of the RNA secondary structure, which the authors annotated with ViennaRNA (RNAfold); and classification of each nucleotide into CDS, 5' UTR or 3' UTR. For a downstream task the authors replace the output layer and fine-tune the model. To find motifs, they use the model's attention contrast matrix with unsupervised hierarchical clustering.

profile.summary: ProtRNA is an RNA language model made by adapting a protein language model, ESM-2, to RNA sequences. The authors' idea is that information learned from the much larger body of protein sequences can transfer to RNA, where sequences are fewer and less conserved. It takes RNA sequences and returns per-nucleotide embeddings, which the repository uses for secondary structure, protein-RNA interaction and mean ribosome loading prediction.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProtRNA starts from the ESM-2 protein language model and is trained further on RNA by a cross-modality transfer learning strategy. In the released code the model keeps the ESM-2 vocabulary of amino acids and appends lower-case RNA tokens (a, u, g, c, x), so the same alphabet holds both kinds of sequence. Input RNA is lower-cased, T is mapped to u, and any other character becomes x. The pretrained model built by the loader has 33 layers, embedding dimension 1280 and 20 attention heads. Embeddings from layer 33 feed separate prediction heads for each downstream task. The sources read do not describe the RNA training objective or data in detail.

profile.summary: RoseTTAFoldNA (also called RF2NA) predicts the three-dimensional structure of proteins, RNA and DNA, alone or bound together in complexes. It takes the sequence of each chain, builds multiple sequence alignments and template searches, and outputs an atomic model in PDB format with per-residue confidence (predicted lDDT) and predicted aligned error. It extends the RoseTTAFold protein structure network to nucleic acids.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README: Inputs, Expected outputs

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RoseTTAFoldNA uses the three-track design of RoseTTAFold, which refines three representations together: the sequence (1D), pairwise distances between residues (2D) and atom coordinates (3D). The authors extended each track to nucleic acids. The 1D track gains 10 tokens for the four DNA and four RNA nucleotides plus unknown DNA and unknown RNA. The 2D track models base-base and base-amino acid interactions. The 3D track places each nucleotide with a frame on its phosphate group and 10 torsion angles. The network has 36 three-track layers and four refinement layers. It was trained on protein monomers and complexes, RNA monomers and dimers, and protein-RNA and protein-DNA complexes from the PDB, with a generalised all-atom FAPE loss, and inputs include MSAs of related protein and nucleic acid sequences.

profile.summary: SpliceAI2 is a deep learning model from Illumina that predicts RNA splicing from genomic sequence. It reads about 200 kb of DNA around a gene and predicts how much each position is used as a splice donor or acceptor, how much each splice junction is used, and the most likely complete transcripts. Comparing predictions for reference and alternate alleles gives a score for how strongly a variant changes splicing.
profile.summary_source_locator: Manuscript: Main 'Hierarchical model of RNA splicing'; Methods 'Variant effect prediction'; README: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input is 196,608 bp of genomic sequence on the gene's sense strand, one-hot encoded, plus a one-hot code for the species (ten channels). A dense layer projects it to 256 channels, and 20 MetaFormer blocks follow, each with a depth-wise dilated convolution and a feed-forward network, at progressively coarser pooling. Each block's output feeds a splice site head over the central 65,536 positions. The 1,024 positions with the highest splice site usage are then paired by a query-key product to give a 1,024 by 1,024 matrix of splice junction usage. Sites and junctions form a splice graph, and Viterbi decoding finds the highest scoring paths, which are the predicted transcripts. The model was trained end-to-end on splice site, junction and transcript usage, with the three losses summed.
sections.source_locator: Manuscript: Methods 'SpliceAI2 model' (Inputs, Architecture, Outputs, Training); 'Transcript prediction'

The released model is an ensemble of two checkpoints trained with identical settings, held on Hugging Face as spliceai2_multispecies_13M_01 and spliceai2_multispecies_13M_02, each with a model.ckpt; the README's commands pass both folders. Illumina also publishes precomputed scores for all possible single nucleotide variants and observed indels in protein-coding genes (GENCODE v48, GRCh38). The manuscript also describes a tissue-specific model conditioned on RBP expression; the files read do not show it as released. profile.summary: GPN-Promoter (Hugging Face name gpn-animal-promoter) is a DNA language model trained on promoter sequences from animal genomes. It was released with TraitGym, a benchmark of causal regulatory variants in human genetics. Given a DNA window, it predicts masked nucleotides; the GPN tools turn this into a variant score, the log-likelihood ratio of the alternate against the reference allele, or into sequence embeddings.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GPN-Promoter belongs to the GPN (GPN-SS) family: single-sequence genomic language models trained on unaligned genomes with masked language modelling. The published config uses the GPN model type with a ByteNet-style convolutional encoder of 64 layers and hidden size 1024, a first kernel size of 9 and later kernel size of 5, with dilation base 2 cycling every 8 layers. The vocabulary has 7 tokens, from the tokenizer gonzalobenegas/tokenizer-dna-mlm named in the training script. The archived training command used a dataset version called v6/512, 64 layers and hidden size 1024, with a total batch size of 2048. For variant scoring, the GPN package compares the model's likelihood of the alternate and reference alleles, averaged over both strands.

profile.summary: CodonBERT is a language model for the coding regions of mRNA, built by Sanofi for mRNA vaccine and therapeutic design. It reads a coding sequence codon by codon and outputs an embedding for each codon. These embeddings can be fine-tuned to predict properties such as protein expression and mRNA degradation, to help choose among the many mRNA sequences that encode the same protein.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CodonBERT is a BERT model of 12 bidirectional transformer encoder layers, each with 12 attention heads and hidden size 768. Each codon is one token: five symbols (A, U, G, C, N) in three positions give 125 codons, plus five special tokens, for a vocabulary of 130. The input is a pair of sequences joined by a separator, embedded with codon, position and segment embeddings. Pretraining combined two tasks: masked language modelling over codons, and sequence taxonomy prediction, in which the model predicts whether the two sequences come from the same one of 14 taxonomic categories. For downstream tasks, the embeddings feed additional trainable layers.

Given an NCBI Taxonomy ID for an organism, it writes new coding sequences for that organism. profile.summary: DGRNA is a pretrained RNA language model built for long RNA sequences. It is built mainly from bidirectional Mamba2 layers rather than the Transformer layers of earlier RNA language models, a choice the authors make to handle long sequences efficiently, and was trained on 100 million RNA sequences. Given RNA sequences, the released code returns a per-position representation that can be used for downstream tasks.

The model is built on the ESM and Fairseq code bases and uses an ESM-1b style alphabet. The released forward pass returns the hidden states, not token logits. profile.summary: EnCodon is a language model for protein-coding DNA that reads a coding sequence one codon at a time and returns a numerical embedding of it. The embeddings can be used as features or fine-tuned, and the package also scores codon variants by comparing model probabilities. It is part of the cdsFM suite, released with the generative model DeCodon, and was pretrained on coding sequences from the NCBI Genomes database.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each token is one of the 64 codons or one of 5 special tokens, and a start token and an end token are added around each sequence. EnCodon is loaded as a masked language model with rotary position embeddings. To embed a sequence, the wrapper runs the model, takes the hidden states of a chosen layer and averages them over the codon positions, leaving out the two special tokens. To score a variant, it compares the log probability of the alternative codon with that of the reference codon, either in the wild-type sequence or with the position masked.

profile.summary: CI-SpliceAI predicts whether a DNA variant disrupts RNA splicing. It keeps the SpliceAI deep convolutional network design but retrains it on manually curated GENCODE splice sites, with all isoforms of a gene collapsed into one, and on all chromosomes. Given a VCF file and a human reference genome, it reports for each variant the predicted gain or loss of acceptor and donor sites and where they occur.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CI-SpliceAI uses the SpliceAI design: five deep convolutional neural networks that label every nucleotide as acceptor, donor or neither, using 10,000 nucleotides of flanking context. For training, GENCODE v37 (GRCh38) transcripts with automated (level 3) annotation were removed, and all remaining splice sites of a gene were merged into one collapsed isoform. Sequences were cut into 15,000-base windows, each predicting 5,000 central nucleotides. The training procedure was reimplemented from SpliceAI, with categorical cross-entropy and the Adam optimiser. The five trained networks are packed into one frozen graph. To score a variant, the tool predicts on the reference and the variant sequence and reports the change (delta score) for acceptor and donor gain and loss.

profile.summary: ERNIE-RNA is a pretrained RNA language model that learns from RNA sequence alone but is given a hint about which bases could pair. It is a modified BERT model whose attention is biased by possible base pairs, trained on 20.4 million non-coding RNA sequences. Given RNA sequences up to 1024 nucleotides, it returns sequence and per-base embeddings and attention maps; the repository also ships fine-tuned heads for secondary structure, 3D closeness and 5' UTR mean ribosome load prediction.

sections.body: ERNIE-RNA follows the BERT design: 12 transformer blocks, each with 12 attention heads over a 768-dimensional token embedding, about 86 million parameters in total. Its change is an all-against-all pairwise bias added to the attention scores, which gives the model prior knowledge of which bases could pair. It was pretrained with masked language modelling: about 15% of nucleotide tokens are replaced and the model predicts them with a cross-entropy loss. The authors report that the attention maps of the pretrained model already capture secondary structure without fine-tuning.

profile.summary: FramePool predicts how strongly a 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) drives translation, measured as mean ribosome load, directly from the 5' UTR sequence. It is a convolutional network trained on a massively parallel reporter assay, made to accept 5' UTRs of any length by pooling motif detections separately in each of the three reading frames. Through Kipoi, it takes variants from a VCF file and reports the predicted log2 fold change in mean ribosome load for each affected 5' UTR.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README; Kipoi model.yaml: info.doc

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: FramePool adapts the published MPRA model of Sample et al. That model used a dense layer, so it only worked for the sequence lengths it was trained on. FramePool keeps three convolutional layers (kernel size 7, 128 filters each, with residual skip connections) and replaces the position-specific dense input with global max and average pooling, done separately for each of the three frames relative to the start codon. The pooled values (a vector of 768) go into a dense layer of 64 neurons and a final linear output. Each model has 282,625 learnable weights; the combined model has 4 more in a scaling layer. The model was trained with the Adam optimiser and a mean squared error loss.
sections.source_locator: README; Paper: Methods, Framepool model; Model training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper trains three models: FramePool50 on 50-nucleotide MPRA sequences, FramePool100 on 25 to 100 nucleotide sequences, and FramePoolCombined on both, with a scaling layer for the two libraries. The paper names FramePoolCombined as the model for variant effect prediction from VCF files. The Kipoi zoo entry downloads the weights file Framepool_combined_residual.h5 from Zenodo record 3584238 with a fixed md5 checksum. A result should name the Kipoi model (Framepool), the weights checksum and the kipoi/models commit; this page read commit 770dcaf2.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Supervised convolutional neural network regression model predicting mean ribosome load from 5' UTR sequence, with a variant effect interface in Kipoi.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Three convolutional layers (kernel size 7, 128 filters, residual skip connections, ReLU), frame pooling (global max and average pooling per reading frame, giving a vector of 768), a dense layer of 64 neurons with dropout 0.2, and a linear output. Implemented in Keras with a TensorFlow backend.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: 5' UTR sequences of any length. In the Kipoi version, a reference and an alternative 5' UTR sequence, built by the dataloader from a BED file of 5' UTR intervals, a reference FASTA and a bgzipped, single-sample, tabix-indexed VCF.
facts.source_locator: Kipoi model.yaml: schema.inputs; Paper: Fig 6 legend; Kipoi page: Make a prediction

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: In Kipoi: the log2 fold change in predicted mean ribosome load caused by the variant, plus the log2 fold change after shifting the frame by 1 and by 2, which can flag variants that create a new in-frame start in the 5' UTR.

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: FramePool50 and FramePool100: 282,625 learnable weights each. FramePoolCombined: 282,625 plus 4 additional learnable weights in the scaling regression layer.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: MPRA data from Sample et al. on an eGFP library in HEK293T cells: 260,000 random 50-nucleotide 5' UTRs with mean ribosome load (20,000 held out for validation), and 76,319 random 5' UTRs of 25 to 100 nucleotides. FramePoolCombined used both training sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model training; Kipoi model.yaml: info.trained_on

facts.label: Known versions
facts.value: FramePool50, FramePool100 and FramePoolCombined in the paper. The Kipoi model Framepool uses the weights file Framepool_combined_residual.h5. The code repository also holds other .h5 model files whose mapping to these names is not documented in the sources read.

facts.label: Training cutoff
facts.value: Not reported. The model was trained on a fixed published MPRA dataset (Sample et al.), and the paper gives no data collection date.

facts.label: Context limits
facts.value: No fixed length: frame pooling lets the model take 5' UTRs of any length. The paper notes that upstream open reading frames longer than the receptive field, 19 nucleotides, cannot be reliably detected.

facts.value: MIT, as declared in the Kipoi model definition and on the Kipoi model page.

strengths.text: Works on 5' UTRs of any length, unlike the fixed-length Optimus models it was adapted from.
Packaged in Kipoi, so variant effects (SNVs and indels) can be scored from a VCF, BED and FASTA with a fixed environment, a test command and Docker images.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Kipoi section; Kipoi page: CLI, docker

strengths.text: Small model: 282,625 learnable weights. On the 20,000 held-out 50-nucleotide MPRA sequences, the authors report a Pearson correlation of 0.964 for FramePool50 against 0.966 for Optimus50.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Results, Evaluating frame pooling on MPRA data

limitations.text: Cannot reliably detect upstream open reading frames longer than 19 nucleotides, and cannot model the order of upstream start sites, so leaky scanning is only partly captured.
Trained on reporter assay data from one cell line (HEK293T, eGFP library), so it predicts the effect of 5' UTR sequence only, without coding sequence or 3' UTR context.
The Kipoi environment pins an old stack: Python 3.7, TensorFlow 1.13.1, Keras 2.2.4 and h5py 2.9.0.

Variant scoring through Kipoi expects a single-sample VCF: the BED and VCF must be sorted with a tabix index, chromosome naming must match across files, and a VCF that mixes patients gives results that are not meaningful.
